content: The Xpert MTB/RIF test is a highly effective diagnostic tool for tuberculosis (TB), particularly when used following chest radiography screening. However, it requires significant resources for implementation. Using chest radiography as a screening method, followed by sputum-smear microscopy, often results in a high proportion of both false-negative and false-positive cases. Many individuals with abnormalities detected on chest radiography may undergo clinical diagnosis, which further increases the number of false-positive cases. The Xpert MTB/RIF test improves the accuracy of TB diagnosis by increasing the number of true cases detected and reducing false-positive cases compared to sputum-smear microscopy. It is the preferred diagnostic test after chest radiography screening. Chest radiography can be used to identify abnormalities indicative of either active or inactive TB. However, some individuals with abnormalities suggestive of inactive TB may actually have active TB. Identifying abnormalities associated with both active and inactive TB is more sensitive but less specific than focusing solely on abnormalities linked to active TB. For guidance on interpreting chest radiographs, the WHO’s Tuberculosis Prevalence Surveys Handbook provides practical advice. Screening for abnormalities suggestive of either active or inactive TB, combined with the Xpert MTB/RIF test, is the most sensitive approach in diagnostic algorithms. This method is particularly critical for high-risk groups where missing TB cases would have significant consequences. However, the positive predictive value of this approach must be considered, and further diagnostic verification may be required in low-prevalence settings. For children under 10 years of age, especially those living with HIV or in contact with TB patients, symptom-based screening should be conducted to identify those with cough, fever, weight loss, or fatigue. Any child with symptoms should be further investigated for TB. Chest radiography may also be added to the initial screening for these children. Abnormalities on chest radiographs suggestive of TB should prompt further investigation to confirm the diagnosis. In children younger than 10 years who are not part of contact investigations or HIV-related screenings, interviews should determine if the child is HIV-positive or has had recent contact with a TB patient. If so, the diagnostic algorithms for high-risk children should be applied. Hilar adenopathy detected on chest radiography in asymptomatic children may indicate a contained TB infection, which might not require treatment for active TB. Using chest radiography as a screening tool necessitates the availability of skilled personnel to interpret the images and conduct follow-up clinical assessments. In resource-limited settings, it may not be feasible to implement algorithms involving chest radiography. No studies have evaluated screening algorithms for children aged 5–15 years or for children under 5 who are not contacts of TB patients or HIV-positive. Symptom screening and chest radiography in young children are likely to have low specificity, as pulmonary TB is a relatively rare cause of respiratory symptoms in this age group. Systematic screening of young children could lead to unnecessary investigations and a high number of false-positive and false-negative cases. The WHO Guideline Development Group advises against general TB screening in children under 10 years, except for those known to be HIV-positive or in contact with TB patients, due to the potential for more harm than benefit. Key indicators for evaluating TB screening programs include the number of individuals eligible for screening, the number screened, the proportion of eligible individuals screened, the number of suspected TB cases identified, the number undergoing diagnostic investigations, the number diagnosed with TB (by type), the proportion of those investigated who have TB, the number needed to screen to detect one TB case, the proportion of initial defaulters (diagnosed but not starting treatment), and treatment success and death rates. Additional data disaggregation by age and sex may be useful but requires detailed data collection. Screening uptake can only be assessed if the size of the target group is well-defined. Routine recording and reporting systems should include logs of the number of people screened in each risk group. Special registers with individual-level data may be used for more detailed analysis, though this is resource-intensive. Programmatic evaluations may be needed to address low screening uptake, unexpected findings, or operational challenges. Monitoring trends over time is essential to reassess the prioritization of risk groups, screening approaches, and intervals. Operational research can complement standard monitoring to improve local screening performance and contribute to the global evidence base. Topics for research include assessing the accuracy of screening algorithms, identifying operational challenges, improving acceptability, and evaluating the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of screening in different settings. Randomized trials are needed to assess the shortand long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of TB screening. Implementing such studies requires careful planning and significant resources.
